notes.meaning: A man named Micah confessed to his mother that he had stolen eleven hundred pieces of silver from her. He only admitted his crime because he was terrified after hearing her speak a curse on the thief. Instead of correcting him, his mother praised him and spoke a blessing to try to cancel her curse.

Micah's mother declared that she was giving all the returned silver to the Lord for her son's benefit. Yet her idea of honoring God was to use the money to make a carved and molten idol. She thought she could serve the true God while openly breaking His command against worshiping images.

Although she had promised all the silver to God, Micah's mother gave only two hundred pieces to a silversmith. The maker fashioned the metal images, and they were placed inside Micah's house. Her actions showed both greed and hypocrisy, since she kept most of the money she had pledged.

Micah set up a private shrine in his home to hold his religious objects. He made an ephod, a special vest copied from the high priest, along with household idols, and ordained his own son as priest. This home-grown religion was completely against God's law, which reserved the priesthood only for Aaron's family.

Israel had no king or judge at this time to uphold the law and hold people accountable. Because there was no government leader, everyone decided for themselves what was right and wrong. When people follow their own desires instead of God's commands, spiritual ruin always follows.

A young man who belonged to the tribe of Levi lived in Bethlehem in the region of Judah. Bethlehem was not one of the cities appointed for the Levites, so he was living there as an outsider. He was already living outside the normal place of service that God had arranged for his tribe.

The young Levite left Bethlehem to wander and look for a new place where he could find a home. In his travels, he came to the hill country of Ephraim and stopped at Micah's house. Instead of serving God faithfully in a designated town, he was roaming the country looking for his own advantage.

Micah asked the traveler where he had come from, and the young man explained his background. He stated that he was a Levite from Bethlehem on the road to settle wherever he could find work. He was essentially marketing his religious status to anyone who would hire him.

Micah asked the young man to stay with him and serve as a spiritual father and family priest. In return, Micah offered him food, a yearly set of clothes, and ten pieces of silver. The young man agreed, treating a sacred calling as nothing more than a paid job for personal security.

The Levite agreed to the terms and moved into Micah's household. Micah treated him warmly and cared for him just like one of his own sons. Both men felt pleased with the arrangement, even though their private sanctuary directly violated God's commands.

Micah performed a ceremony to ordain the Levite as his personal priest, and the young man settled into the home. Micah had no legal right to appoint anyone, and the Levite was not from the family of Aaron. Both men acted with great presumption by inventing their own religious authority.

Micah foolishly believed that having an actual Levite in his home guaranteed that the Lord would bless him. He thought an outward religious ritual would make God happy, even though his shrine was full of forbidden idols and a fake priesthood. Sincerity can never make up for disobeying God's truth.
